milestones.name: Bucktown, Maryland
milestones.postcard: Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County around 1822. She worked these fields and forests as a child, learning the land she would later cross in the dark.

milestones.name: Cambridge, Maryland
milestones.postcard: Cambridge, on the Choptank River, was the county seat, where enslaved people were bought and sold. Fear of being sold away from family drove many to risk everything to go north.

milestones.name: Poplar Neck, Caroline County
milestones.postcard: In the fall of 1849 Tubman left from near here, travelling at night and guided by the North Star. She would return about thirteen times to lead roughly seventy family members and friends to freedom.

milestones.name: Along the Choptank
milestones.postcard: Rivers and creeks were roads for freedom seekers: water hid tracks, and following it north kept them on course.

milestones.name: Camden, Delaware
milestones.postcard: Delaware was a slave state, but Quaker communities like Camden's included people who sheltered and guided freedom seekers.

milestones.name: Dover, Delaware
milestones.postcard: Slave catchers watched the roads through Dover. In 1857 the 'Dover Eight', guided by Tubman's network, fought their way out of the town jail where they'd been betrayed, and continued north.

milestones.name: Odessa, Delaware
milestones.postcard: By local tradition, the Appoquinimink Friends Meeting House here hid freedom seekers in its loft.

milestones.name: New Castle, Delaware
milestones.postcard: In 1848 Quaker abolitionists Thomas Garrett and John Hunn were tried here and fined so heavily for aiding freedom seekers that it took most of what they owned. Garrett told the court he would keep helping anyway.

milestones.name: Wilmington, Delaware
milestones.postcard: Thomas Garrett's home was one of the last stops before free soil. He is credited with helping over 2,500 people, Tubman among them many times.

milestones.name: The Pennsylvania line
milestones.postcard: Crossing into Pennsylvania meant entering a free state. But after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, no Northern state was truly safe, and many kept going to Canada.

milestones.name: Chester, Pennsylvania
milestones.postcard: Black and white abolitionists in Chester and Delaware County passed freedom seekers on toward Philadelphia.

milestones.name: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
milestones.postcard: William Still of the Philadelphia Vigilance Committee interviewed hundreds of freedom seekers and wrote down their stories, so they wouldn't be forgotten. Tubman lived and worked here after 1849. Chapter 1 complete.

freedom.teaser: Harriet Tubman's corridor north through the Delmarva Peninsula.
facts: c. 1822: Araminta Ross is born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland.
1849: She escapes alone, following the North Star, and takes the name Harriet Tubman.
1850s: She returns about 13 times and guides roughly 70 people to freedom.
1863: She leads the Combahee River Raid in the Civil War, freeing more than 700 people.
freedom.why: The original act of walking toward freedom, at night, unseen.

freedom.title: The North Star
freedom.subtitle: Chapter 2 · Philadelphia to St. Catharines
freedom.teaser: Through New York to Canada, where Tubman settled the families she led to freedom.
facts: 1850: The Fugitive Slave Act makes freedom seekers unsafe anywhere in the US.
1851–1858: Tubman bases herself in St. Catharines, Ontario, beyond US law.
Routes ran through New York State, often via Rochester, to the Niagara crossing.
freedom.why: When the law follows you, keep walking until it can't.

freedom.title: The Silk Road
freedom.subtitle: Chang'an to Constantinople · the real distance
freedom.teaser: About 6,400 km of caravan routes that carried silk, paper, religions and ideas between China and the Mediterranean.
facts: c. 138–126 BCE: Han envoy Zhang Qian's missions west open the routes to China's court.
Goods moved in relays; few traders ever walked the whole way.
Paper, papermaking and Buddhism travelled it; so did the plague in the 1300s.
1877: German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coins the name "Silk Road".
freedom.why: The longest walk on the list, measured at its real-world length.

freedom.title: Disguised as a Sailor
freedom.subtitle: Frederick Douglass · Baltimore to New York, 1838
freedom.teaser: Borrowed papers, a sailor's clothes, one train ride. He became the century's great voice against slavery.
facts: Sept 3, 1838: Dressed as a sailor, carrying a free Black seaman's papers, he boards a train in Baltimore.
By train and steamboat via Wilmington and Philadelphia, he reaches New York in under 24 hours.
Anna Murray, who helped fund the escape, joins him; they marry days later.
1845: He publishes his Narrative, an instant bestseller.
freedom.why: Courage plus a convincing disguise: an early lesson in operational security.

freedom.title: Bloody Sunday to the Capitol
freedom.subtitle: Selma to Montgomery, 1965
freedom.teaser: Turned back on the Edmund Pettus Bridge, the marchers came back and walked all 87 km for the vote.
facts: Mar 7, 1965: State troopers attack marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge ("Bloody Sunday").
Mar 21–25: Thousands walk 54 miles (87 km) from Selma to the Alabama Capitol.
Aug 6, 1965: The Voting Rights Act is signed into law.
freedom.why: A walk that changed the law.

freedom.title: The Enchantress of Numbers
freedom.subtitle: Ada Lovelace · London
freedom.teaser: In 1843 she published the first algorithm meant for a machine, a century before computers existed.
facts: 1815: Born Augusta Ada Byron, daughter of the poet Lord Byron.
1843: Her Notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine include "Note G", a method for computing Bernoulli numbers.
She saw that such a machine could work with symbols, music even, not just numbers.
freedom.why: Every app, this one included, descends from her notes.

freedom.title: Amazing Grace
freedom.subtitle: Grace Hopper · Harvard to the Pentagon
freedom.teaser: She built the first compiler and taught computers to read something close to English.
facts: 1947: Her team tapes a moth into the Harvard Mark II log: the "first actual case of bug being found".
1952: She builds the A-0, one of the first compilers.
1959: Her work leads to COBOL, still running banks today.
freedom.why: Making machines speak human was its own kind of liberation.

freedom.title: Breaking Enigma
freedom.subtitle: Alan Turing · Bletchley Park to Manchester
freedom.teaser: He cracked the codes that shortened a war and wrote the theory every computer runs on.
facts: 1936: "On Computable Numbers" defines the universal machine.
1939–1945: At Bletchley Park his Bombe design helps break German Enigma traffic.
1952: Prosecuted for homosexuality; he dies in 1954. Royal pardon in 2013.
freedom.why: The father of computer science, persecuted for his private life.

freedom.title: The 2600 Hz Whistle
freedom.subtitle: Phone phreaks · "Captain Crunch"
freedom.teaser: A toy whistle from a cereal box could seize the phone network. Hacking culture starts here.
facts: 1960s: Phreaks discover the network's 2600 Hz control tone; a Cap'n Crunch prize whistle can play it.
John Draper takes the nickname "Captain Crunch".
1971: Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs build and sell "blue boxes" before founding Apple.
freedom.why: Curiosity about how systems really work: the root of hacker culture.

freedom.title: New Directions
freedom.subtitle: Whitfield Diffie & Martin Hellman · Stanford, 1976
freedom.teaser: Two strangers can agree on a secret in public. Their paper made private internet traffic possible.
facts: 1976: "New Directions in Cryptography" introduces public-key key exchange.
Ralph Merkle's earlier work on public key distribution fed into the same idea.
2015: Diffie and Hellman receive the Turing Award.
freedom.why: Every padlock in your browser, and your phone talking to us over Tor, starts here.

freedom.title: We Got Him?
freedom.subtitle: Rivest, Shamir & Adleman · MIT, 1977
freedom.teaser: Three researchers found the first practical public-key cipher. A British spy had found it first, in secret.
facts: 1973: At GCHQ, Clifford Cocks devises the same idea; it stays classified until 1997.
1977: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman publish RSA at MIT.
1977: Martin Gardner's Scientific American column sets the RSA-129 challenge.
1994: RSA-129 falls to volunteers worldwide: "The Magic Words Are Squeamish Ossifrage".
freedom.why: Public math versus secret math, and the public won the credit.

freedom.title: Pretty Good Privacy
freedom.subtitle: Phil Zimmermann · 1991
freedom.teaser: He gave the world strong encryption for free, and was investigated for 'exporting munitions' for it.
facts: 1991: Zimmermann releases PGP; it spreads worldwide over the internet.
1993–1996: US authorities investigate him for exporting cryptography; the case is dropped.
1995: PGP's source code is published as a printed book, protected as speech, to get it abroad.
freedom.why: Privacy for everyone, not just governments.

freedom.title: Cypherpunks Write Code
freedom.subtitle: The cypherpunk mailing list · 1992
freedom.teaser: A mailing list of cryptographers decided privacy wouldn't be granted, it would be built.
facts: 1992: Eric Hughes, Timothy C. May and John Gilmore start the cypherpunks list.
1993: Hughes writes "A Cypherpunk's Manifesto": "Cypherpunks write code."
The list incubates anonymous remailers, digital cash and early Tor-era ideas.
freedom.why: VeilWalker's whole philosophy in one sentence.

freedom.title: The Dead Cow Walk
freedom.subtitle: Cult of the Dead Cow · Lubbock to DEF CON
freedom.teaser: Texas teenagers founded a hacker collective that gave the world Back Orifice and the word "hacktivism".
facts: 1984: cDc is founded in Lubbock, Texas.
1996: cDc member Omega coins "hacktivism".
1998: Back Orifice is unveiled at DEF CON 6 to expose Windows security flaws.
freedom.why: Hacking as protest and as public-interest security research.

freedom.title: The Condor
freedom.subtitle: Kevin Mitnick · a DEF CON walk
freedom.teaser: Once the most wanted computer hacker in America, later the person companies paid to break in.
facts: Best known for social engineering: talking people out of passwords and access.
Feb 1995: Arrested in Raleigh, North Carolina after years as a fugitive; "Free Kevin" campaigns follow.
2000: Released; he becomes a security consultant and author (Ghost in the Wires, 2011).
2023: Dies in July.
freedom.why: The human is usually the weakest link. Guard your 24 words.

freedom.title: We Are Legion
freedom.subtitle: Anonymous · Project Chanology, 2008
freedom.teaser: An imageboard in-joke turned into a global street protest behind Guy Fawkes masks.
facts: Mid-2000s: Anonymous emerges from the 4chan imageboard culture.
Jan 2008: The Church of Scientology moves to suppress a leaked Tom Cruise video; Anonymous responds.
Feb 10, 2008: Project Chanology street protests in cities worldwide; Guy Fawkes masks become the symbol.
freedom.why: The first time an anonymous online collective walked into the streets.

freedom.title: The Genesis Block
freedom.subtitle: Satoshi Nakamoto · 21 km for 21 million
freedom.teaser: A pseudonymous author published nine pages, mined block zero, then vanished.
facts: Oct 31, 2008: The Bitcoin whitepaper is posted to a cryptography mailing list.
Jan 3, 2009: The genesis block embeds a headline: "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks".
2011: Satoshi's last known messages; the author's identity remains unknown.
The supply is capped at 21 million coins, hence the 21 km.
freedom.why: Proof that a pseudonym can change the world. VeilWalker's ledger is built the same chained, signed way.

freedom.title: The Wall Trail
freedom.subtitle: Berlin · 1961–1989
freedom.teaser: Walk the line where the Berlin Wall stood, past the places people risked everything to cross.
facts: Aug 13, 1961: The Wall goes up overnight around West Berlin.
At least 140 people are killed at the Wall trying to cross or in connection with it.
Nov 9, 1989: The Wall opens. Today the Mauerweg trail follows its path.
freedom.why: A border built to stop people walking, and the day they walked through it.

freedom.title: The Whistleblower Trail
freedom.subtitle: Hong Kong · June 2013
freedom.teaser: A contractor walked out with proof of mass surveillance and changed how the world thinks about privacy.
facts: June 2013: In Hong Kong, NSA contractor Edward Snowden gives journalists documents on mass surveillance.
Reporting reveals programs such as PRISM and bulk phone-record collection.
2015: The USA FREEDOM Act ends bulk collection of Americans' phone records by the NSA.
freedom.why: Why Tor-by-default matters.

freedom.title: The Motorcycle Diaries
freedom.subtitle: Che Guevara · Buenos Aires to Caracas, 1952
freedom.teaser: The journey across South America that turned a medical student into a revolutionary. Told honestly, controversies included.
facts: 1952: Ernesto Guevara and Alberto Granado ride a 1939 Norton ("La Poderosa") north from Argentina.
The poverty he saw on the road shaped his politics.
Later a leader of the Cuban Revolution; he oversaw executions at La Cabaña prison, which critics condemn.
1967: Captured and executed in Bolivia. Admired by some, condemned by others.
freedom.why: A journey that changed a person; history shown with its contradictions.

volumes: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took
OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.title: The Cutpurse
cards.subtitle: Mary Frith, "Moll Cutpurse" · London, c. 1584–1659

card.name: Moll Cutpurse
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: Pickpocket, fence and the most talked-about woman in Jacobean London's underworld.
facts: c. 1584: Mary Frith is born in London.
She works the crowded streets as a cutpurse, then runs a business returning stolen goods to their owners, for a fee.
She walks the city in men's clothing, scandalous at the time.
1611: Middleton and Dekker put her on stage in the play The Roaring Girl.
1612: Made to do public penance at St Paul's Cross.
1659: Dies in London.
cards.why: A life lived on foot in packed streets, reading crowds the way we read networks.

cards.title: The Con Artist
cards.subtitle: "Count" Victor Lustig · Paris & New York, 1890–1947

card.name: Victor Lustig
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower to a scrap dealer, then walked out of a federal jail.
facts: 1890: Born in Austria-Hungary.
1925: Posing as a French official, he 'sells' the Eiffel Tower for scrap to a dealer who is too embarrassed to report it.
He also cons Al Capone, and later runs a large counterfeiting operation.
Sept 1935: Escapes the Federal Detention Headquarters in Manhattan down a rope of bedsheets, reportedly posing as a window washer.
Caught in Pittsburgh about a month later; dies in federal custody in 1947.
cards.why: Social engineering, decades before the word. And one very public walk away.

cards.title: The Ghost of the Louvre
cards.subtitle: Vincenzo Peruggia · Paris, 1911

card.name: Vincenzo Peruggia
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took
card.quote: The greatest escape can look ordinary.

cards.teaser: Art thief. He walked out of the Louvre with the Mona Lisa under his work smock.
facts: Aug 21, 1911: On a Monday, when the Louvre is closed, Peruggia, a former museum worker, takes the Mona Lisa off the wall.
Dressed like the museum's workmen, he hides the panel under his smock and walks out.
The painting sits in his Paris room for more than two years.
Dec 1913: Arrested in Florence trying to sell it; the painting goes home to the Louvre.
He serves only months in prison and is seen as a patriot by some Italians.
cards.why: No disguise beats looking like you belong there.

cards.title: The Master Forger
cards.subtitle: Han van Meegeren · Netherlands, 1889–1947

card.name: Han van Meegeren
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: He forged Vermeers so well that one hung in Hermann Göring's collection.
facts: 1889: Born in Deventer, Netherlands.
1930s–40s: Paints fake Vermeers that fool leading experts and sell for fortunes.
One, Christ and the Adulteress, is bought by Nazi leader Hermann Göring.
1945: Arrested for treason for selling a national treasure to the Nazis.
To prove it was a fake, he paints another 'Vermeer' in front of witnesses.
1947: Convicted of forgery instead; dies weeks later.
cards.why: Proof of work, literally. The card for anyone who has had to prove what's real.

cards.title: The Escapist
cards.subtitle: Jack Sheppard · London, 1702–1724

card.name: Jack Sheppard
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: Four escapes in one year, twice out of Newgate, the most secure prison in London.
facts: 1702: Born in Spitalfields, London; apprenticed as a carpenter.
1724: Arrested for theft and burglary, he escapes custody four times in a single year.
Oct 1724: Chained in Newgate's strongest room, he climbs up a chimney and out across the rooftops.
Recaptured days later, drunk, walking the city in fine clothes.
Nov 16, 1724: Hanged at Tyburn, before a crowd reported at 200,000.
cards.why: Every lock is a puzzle. He kept walking out until they stopped him for good.

cards.title: The Coast Runner
cards.subtitle: Jack Rattenbury · Beer, Devon, 1778–1844

card.name: Jack Rattenbury
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: The "Rob Roy of the West": smuggler, pilot and fisherman on the Devon cliffs.
facts: 1778: Born in the fishing village of Beer, Devon.
Goes to sea at 9; starts smuggling at about 16.
Contraband is hidden in places like the Beer Quarry Caves, out of sight of the excise men.
Caught and escaped many times, by his own account.
1837: Dictates Memoirs of a Smuggler; buried in Seaton churchyard in 1844.
cards.why: Cliff paths at night, carrying what the government said you couldn't.

cards.title: The Smuggler King
cards.subtitle: Isaac Gulliver · Dorset, 1745–1822

card.name: Isaac Gulliver
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: Ran one of the largest contraband networks on England's south coast, and died rich.
facts: 1745: Born in Wiltshire.
Builds a smuggling operation moving tea, gin and lace through Dorset's coast and inland routes.
Reputed never to have killed anyone: the "gentle smuggler".
Later a respected landowner and banker; dies in Wimborne in 1822.
cards.why: A whole network of paths and trusted couriers: the original distributed system.

cards.title: The Iron Walker
cards.subtitle: Ned Kelly · Victoria, Australia, 1854–1880

card.name: Ned Kelly
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol I: The Roads They Took

cards.teaser: At his last stand he walked toward the police in about 40 kg of homemade iron armour.
facts: 1854: Born in Victoria to an Irish convict father.
1878–1880: The Kelly Gang robs banks while the colony hunts them.
June 28, 1880: At Glenrowan, Kelly advances on foot at dawn in plough-steel armour.
Shot in his unprotected legs, he is captured.
Nov 11, 1880: Hanged at Melbourne Gaol.
cards.why: The heaviest walk on the list. Some steps cost more than others.

cards.title: The Mountain Queen
cards.subtitle: Maggie Bailey · Harlan County, Kentucky, 1904–2005

card.name: Maggie Bailey
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: Sold moonshine from her mountain home for about 80 years.
facts: 1904: Born in Harlan County, Kentucky.
Starts selling moonshine at 17, in a dry county, and keeps going into her 90s.
Taken to court again and again; only one federal conviction, in 1941.
Dec 2005: Dies at 101, "Queen of the Mountain Bootleggers".
cards.why: Appalachian hollows were walked, not driven.

cards.title: The Bahamas Queen
cards.subtitle: Gertrude "Cleo" Lythgoe · Nassau, 1888–1974

card.name: Gertrude Lythgoe
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: The only woman with a wholesale liquor licence in Nassau, supplying Rum Row.
facts: 1888: Born in Ohio.
1920s: Runs a liquor export business from Nassau in the Bahamas, legally, just out of US reach.
Her stock supplies the rum-runners anchored off the US coast: Rum Row.
1964: Publishes her memoir, The Bahama Queen. Dies in 1974.
cards.why: Jurisdiction is a map. She stood on the right side of the line.

cards.title: The Real McCoy
cards.subtitle: Bill McCoy · Atlantic Coast, 1877–1948

card.name: Bill McCoy
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: Pioneer of Rum Row: ships full of liquor parked just past US waters.
facts: 1877: Born in Syracuse, New York.
1920s: Sails his schooner Arethusa (later Tomoka) loaded with whiskey to the edge of US waters.
Known for never watering down his liquor; the phrase "the real McCoy" is often tied to him, though it is older.
1923: His ship is seized by the Coast Guard; he serves nine months.
cards.why: Honest goods in a dishonest trade. Reputation was the only trust layer.

cards.title: The Shore Runner
cards.subtitle: Long Island Rum Row · 1920s · historical archetype

card.name: The Shore Runner
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: A made-up character standing for the crews who carried liquor ashore on Long Island.
facts: 1920–1933: Liquor ships wait offshore; fast boats run cases to Long Island beaches at night.
Landing spots included the South Shore and the East End around Montauk and the North Fork.
From the beach, cases went by foot, cart and truck to New York City.
This card is fictional: it honours the unnamed people who did the carrying.
cards.why: History remembers the bosses. This one is for the people who walked the cargo up the beach.

cards.title: The Last Moonshiner
cards.subtitle: Marvin "Popcorn" Sutton · Appalachia, 1946–2009

card.name: Popcorn Sutton
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: Legacy outlaw: still making mountain moonshine decades after Prohibition ended.
facts: 1946: Born in Maggie Valley, North Carolina, into a moonshining family.
Makes whiskey in the Smoky Mountains the old way, and becomes a folk hero on film.
2008: Federal agents find large stills and hundreds of gallons of liquor.
2009: Dies shortly before he was due to report to federal prison.
cards.why: Legacy card: the trade outlived the law that created it.

cards.title: The Beer Baron
cards.subtitle: Dutch Schultz · The Bronx, New York, 1901–1935

card.name: Dutch Schultz
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: Ran beer through the Bronx and Harlem, then fought the government and the Mob at once.
facts: 1901: Born Arthur Flegenheimer in New York.
1920s: Builds a beer empire in the Bronx, reportedly with operations as far off as the Catskills.
1935: Tried for tax evasion upstate: a hung jury in Syracuse, then acquittal in Malone.
Oct 1935: Shot in Newark by fellow gangsters; dies the next day.
cards.why: The streets of the Bronx, block by block.

cards.title: The King of Chicago
cards.subtitle: Al Capone · Chicago, 1899–1947

card.name: Al Capone
card.collection: OUTLAWS ON FOOT · Vol II: The Dry Years

cards.teaser: Boss card. The most notorious bootlegger of all, brought down by his tax returns.
facts: 1899: Born in Brooklyn, New York.
1920s: Runs the Chicago Outfit's bootlegging, gambling and brothels.
1929: The St. Valentine's Day Massacre is widely blamed on his gang.
1931: Convicted of tax evasion; sentenced to 11 years, later served partly in Alcatraz.
1947: Dies in Florida.
cards.why: The boss card: collect everyone else first. Even kings get caught by paperwork.

peaks.title: HIDDEN PEAKS · climb counts only on freezing walks

all.name: Mount Kosciuszko
facts: Australia's highest point, and the easiest of the Seven Summits.
1840: Named by Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki after freedom fighter Tadeusz Kościuszko.
Some climbers count Puncak Jaya as Oceania's summit instead; this deck has both.

all.name: Mount Baker
facts: Koma Kulshan to the Lummi and Nooksack peoples; an active, glacier-covered volcano.
1868: First recorded ascent, by Edmund Coleman's party.
1998–99: The Mt. Baker ski area recorded 1,140 inches of snow, a world record for one season.

all.name: Mount Rainier
facts: Tahoma (or Tacoma) to the Puyallup and other Coast Salish peoples; 14,410 ft.
The most glaciated peak in the contiguous United States, and an active volcano.
1870: First recorded ascent, by Hazard Stevens and Philemon Van Trump.

all.name: Puncak Jaya
facts: Also called Carstensz Pyramid: the highest island peak in the world.
Its small glaciers sit almost on the equator and are shrinking fast.
1962: First ascent, by Heinrich Harrer's team (of Seven Years in Tibet).

all.name: Vinson Massif
facts: The highest point in Antarctica, about 1,200 km from the South Pole.
First seen from the air only in 1958.
Dec 1966: First ascent, by an American expedition led by Nicholas Clinch.

all.name: Mount Elbrus
facts: A dormant volcano with twin summits; the west summit is the higher.
1829: First ascent of the east summit, credited to Khillar Khachirov.
1874: A British party led by Florence Crauford Grove reaches the west summit.

all.name: Kilimanjaro
facts: The highest free-standing mountain on Earth, rising from the African plains.
1889: First recorded ascent, by Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller, guided by Yohani Lauwo.
Climbers pass through rainforest, moorland and alpine desert to reach the snow.

all.name: Denali · Mount McKinley
facts: One mountain, two names: Denali ("the high one" in Koyukon) and Mount McKinley.
1917: Federally named McKinley; 2015: renamed Denali; 2025: federally McKinley again. Alaska keeps Denali.
1913: First ascent, by Hudson Stuck, Harry Karstens, Robert Tatum and Walter Harper, the first to the top.
Measured base to peak, it's taller than Everest.

all.name: Aconcagua
facts: The highest mountain outside Asia, in the Andes.
1897: First recorded ascent, by Swiss guide Matthias Zurbriggen.
An Inca mummy found on its slopes shows people climbed high here long before.

all.name: K2 · The Savage Mountain
all.quote: Do what thou wilt. The mountain will too.
facts: The second-highest mountain on Earth, and by far the deadlier of the two highest.
1902: Oscar Eckenstein and Aleister Crowley lead the first serious attempt, reaching about 6,500 m.
Crowley, the occultist later called "the wickedest man in the world", went on to lead a 1905 Kangchenjunga attempt.
1954: First ascent, by Italians Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni.
Jan 2021: A team of ten Nepali climbers makes the first winter ascent.

all.name: Mount Everest
all.quote: The roof of the world. You walked here.
facts: Chomolungma in Tibetan, Sagarmatha in Nepali; 8,849 m by the 2020 China–Nepal survey.
May 29, 1953: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reach the summit.
The end of the deck: climb its height on freezing walks and you've climbed Everest.
